LLM auditresponse for xvfb-run:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This is the well-known upstream `xvfb-run` helper script from xorg-server (Debian/T2 SDE lineage), shipped by the xlibre-xserver package to run a command inside a virtual X server. Its behavior matches its stated purpose exactly: parse options with `getopt`, allocate a free display number, create a temporary directory via `mktemp --directory --tmpdir`, start `Xvfb` on that display with `-nolisten tcp` by default, install a locally generated `mcookie` into a throwaway `XAUTHORITY` file, execute the caller-supplied command with `DISPLAY` set, kill the Xvfb PID, remove the temp directory, and propagate the command's exit status.

Nothing in the file performs network I/O, downloads code, or touches data outside its own scope. The only `eval` is `eval set -- "$ARGS"`, the canonical idiom for re-parsing `getopt` output safely, and it is not fed any remote or decoded content. The single `xauth source -` call reads the authorization entry from a here-doc containing only the freshly generated cookie for the local display. File operations are confined to `/tmp/.X*-lock` probes and the `mktemp` directory it creates and later `rm -r`s. There is no base64/hex/octal decoding, no `curl`/`wget`, no `chmod +x`, no shell reverse shell, and no reference to `PKGBUILD`-adjacent maintainer automation.

The only items worth noting as hygiene rather than security concerns: the script quotes `$XVFBARGS` and `$LISTENTCP` unquoted when expanding them into the `Xvfb` command line, so user-supplied `--server-args` undergo word splitting, and the default `-f` auth-file path (per the usage text) can fall back to `./.Xauthority` when `mktemp` behavior differs. Both are upstream design choices in a locally invoked utility, not evidence of injected malicious code, so the file is assessed as SAFE.
</details>
<evidence></evidence>
<summary>Standard upstream xvfb-run helper script; no malicious behavior found.</summary>
</security_assessment>
